title: Claude +Three.js feels like cheating
author: Donkeytonk
selftext:
100% vibe coded this destruction game with Three.js + Rapier physics. 

This was my first fully vibe-coded game and I started with a room and just played around with smashing cubes until it felt fun.

Spent a lot of time going deep into optimization so the physics so this can perform decently in a browser.

The hardest part so far onboarding. Some of the mechanics in this are quite new so I'm trying to find ways to teach destruciton-based beat smashing since I think it's a pretty novel concept.

Inspired heavily by lots of of games - ARMS, DK Bonanza, old school NES games, Taiko drum master and more.

replies.author: Donkeytonk
replies.body:
Everything was prompted with Claude so materials, UI, artwork, structures, level arrangements, music, sound effects, animations are all scripted and procedurally generated. It means the game is lighting quick since it technically holds almost no assets except for a bunch of json files. A lot of effort went into making everything look and feel 8bit in vibe.

I actually spent a lot of time creating all these systems and tools for myself and then made them into a kind of UGC mode so players can prompt their own levels that have unique 8bit sounding music.

replies.author: Donkeytonk
replies.body:
I used to make Roblox games so I learned some coding from that but wasn't very advanced. I started properly vibecoding about 1 month ago. I was lucky I was in a room full of cracked game developers all building with AI so I got a sense of what was possible. 

I gave my self some pretty hard constraints here by keeping everything 8bit style which helped when it came to defining styles. I basically built everything up step by step but had an idea in my mind roughly where I was heading and some of the principles I wanted to keep to. I just kept iterating and optimizing. replies.author: Donkeytonk
replies.body:
Spent 2 days to make the demo ready and submitted for vibejam. That version had 10 levels and the normal fists, all the destruction and core rhythm mechanics were in place, the procedural level/music creation framework (which I used to make those 10 levels but used as a foundation for the UGC mode I added), also all the level complete celebrations etc

The rest of the 10-12 days or so spent on this went into adding another 20 levels, added 10 or so new level styles (different color palettes, lighting/atmosphere for each) adding new unlockable for equipping (rocket fists for example) creating an isometric pixel preview of levels, a community mode where you can generate levels with prompts or play other creator’s levels plus lot’s of small optimization and polish to the gameplay (such as audio calibration, scoring logic for higher level streaks, special rainbow mode for 50+ streak).

I also spent a lot of time testing the UGC mode by making levels, so technically I made about another 150 levels over that two week period but they are counted as community levels but made by myself.

comments.author: presentsq
comments.body: This is very cool. Did you create the sound effects and music with claude too?

replies.author: Donkeytonk
replies.body:
Yes, I had a strict scheme I needed for each song. They had to be same length in terms of beats and phases. And the second half of the track needed to be a more intense version of the first half. There are other motifs and constraints that went into each track. Subtle Microtonal notes get applied, for example, something I got inspired by a canadian band called Angine de Poitrine. Drops always happen in certain phases. I restrict scales to western ones. Plus a bunch of other decisions that make each track feel like they're part of a purposely created soundtrack.

The actual rendering of each track and sound effect is done at run time with Web Audio. I roughly tried to emulate the type of sound you might expect from an NES. In the create-mode, I have a "modern retro mode" where I allow more modern types of sounds to be sythsized like 808 drums, reverb effects etc. The original 30 levels in the first 3 worlds all use the classic mode so sound rougfhly like an original NES but the UGC mode will have a lot more creative diversity. Some sound effects have a bit of extra creative license too with bit crushers, multi timbre etc. I wanted the smashes to sound distinct from the music of each levels and exist in their own layer so they didn't merge into the main music and get lost by the player's ears. The best analogy I can think of here is when you lay a 2d platformer, designers will purposely make the platforms you can collide with in a slightly different style so you can judge what is decorative and what is interactive.

Things like the BPM, scales, key, chord progressions etc are all use in some form in the gameplay. When you punch an object for example, the sound plays in key with the song, so it sounds like it's complimenting the main track. The note of the sound effect is essentially manipulated on the fly to sound musical. The notes you play with your fists will be different depending on the track being played in each level. Also, things like the sound of rubble, coin charges, coin counter and soem other elements are quantized to the beat so they sound rhythmic as you play. The coins for example add a kind of increasingly percussive layer to the track as you increase your streak and more coins are released per smash. Those coins also are in key with the current chord progression / scale so they sound melodically percussive. 

Anyway, all these ideas then went into the music generator in create-mode. The level gets produced first and then based on both the prompt and the level that was generated, a suitable song is produced. For exxample if you have towers that go into the sky, you might get more floaty, chilled songs. If you create an army of evil robots in a gabba rave, you'll get some 180 BPM style robotic music. I even tested making levels set in a jazz bar giraffes playing trumpets and the level delivered with a line of smashable giraffes on stage and some jazzy sounding big band music with lot's of swing was made, all 8bit in style of course.

replies.author: Donkeytonk
replies.body:
The first 30 levels used what is essentially the “Classic 8 bit Mode” you can find in the create mode. It uses the sound generation schema I originally used with Claud as I made each of those levels. As I was making them, I told Claude to remember the schema because we’ll use it later. Levels 11 to 30 were made in level+soundtrack pairs by spinning up two agents for each level. First agent made the level and second agent made the music based on the prompt plus music I fed Claude.

Levels 1 to 10 originally only had one track in the demo I submitted to a vibejam (only had 2 days to get it ready). So once I came back and made the rest of the levels and the UGC mode a week later, I had to retroactively apply the music generator to those levels. This levels were made according to a schema so the music agent checked the level structures and made an attempt to make a suitable song based on the level layout. Did a pretty decent job. Worlds 2 and 3 songs are far better though, since I introduced a lot more thematic elements - volcanic levels, desert levels, ghost houses etc 

Once I started work on the Create mode, I wanted to get more variety in the song outputs since I assumed players might experiment with more varied themes. I was in two minds since this mode sounded a bit more modern but in the end I just decided to have both modes selectable. I prefer modern retro mode personally.
